strengths: The paper offers a useful empirical contribution to vision-language data curation: naturally multilingual captions can provide complementary visual information for the same images. This insight has practical value without requiring a new architecture or benchmark-leading performance.

The central diversity trend appears in human XM annotations across seven languages and in two captioning systems. The matched-caption-count comparisons and shared annotation instructions are sensible controls. Table 3 provides particularly useful grounding: Vertex's coverage of annotated Visual Genome objects increases from 9.6% with three English captions to 11.7% with English/French/Chinese captions.

The supplementary human study supplies additional supporting evidence: 10 English and 10 Japanese speakers caption 30 images, with multilingual combinations covering 8.4% more objects. Translation evaluation by 15 speakers, yielding a reported mean quality of 4.68/5, is also a meaningful safeguard.

The semantic/expressive distinction provides an understandable analytical framework. Translating all fine-tuning targets into English usefully separates caption-source differences from the model's ability to generate different output languages.
weaknesses: The fine-tuning evidence contains consequential reporting inconsistencies. All 36 entries in Table 14, attributed to LLaVA captions, exactly reproduce the corresponding entries in Table 4, attributed to Vertex captions. Independent replication across these sources therefore cannot be verified from the manuscript. Table 15 also contradicts universal same-language superiority: Chinese-trained GIT scores 0.124 on Chinese references, versus 0.131 for multilingual training. Table 10 labels multilingual training best on the mixed test set, although French training performs better in Tables 4, 14, and 15.

Several reported effect sizes have inconsistent baselines or arithmetic. The 46.0%, 66.1%, and 66.8% gains correspond to Table 1's multilingual-versus-monolingual averages, although the introduction attributes them to comparison with English-only captions. Table 2 reports a Vertex monolingual attribute average of 1.98, while its seven listed values average approximately 1.69. These errors do not reverse the diversity trend, but weaken confidence in its reported magnitude.

The measurement pipeline is incompletely validated. The translation audit in Section 8.1 samples model-generated captions, not XM human annotations, and evaluates conceptual preservation rather than preservation of tone or authenticity. Near-chance language prediction by one classifier does not establish the absence of translation artifacts. Scene-graph extraction and canonicalization accuracy are not quantified, and Visual Genome object recall does not validate the additional attributes, relations, or overall factual precision.

Some interpretations exceed the experimental design. Section 3.2's comparison of cross-language and cross-model diversity cannot rule out language-specific model modes: no justified relationship between these two sources of variation is established. Speaker-population differences and uncontrolled caption length also limit attribution to perceptual differences. The fine-tuning experiments demonstrate adaptation to caption distributions, but do not establish improved visual representations or robustness.

Reproducibility is limited by missing fine-tuning hyperparameters, precise LLaVA checkpoint and decoding settings, and concept-merging thresholds. The primary coverage and fine-tuning tables lack uncertainty estimates or repeated-run results. The repeated, grounded coverage findings provide a credible contribution, but unresolved experimental inconsistencies and measurement limitations keep my assessment at the decision boundary.
